opening: Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang and its shares jumped by almost a third, lifting markets from Wall Street to Seoul. Iran said it will not negotiate until its conditions are met, NATO sent Poland an early-warning aircraft, and drones again struck Sudan’s capital.

stories.title: Nvidia brings back Jensen Huang as chief executive, and its shares jump by almost a third, lifting markets from New York to Seoul
stories.body: Nvidia’s board voted unanimously on Monday to reinstate Jensen Huang as president and chief executive, less than two weeks after he resigned amid reports of an affair with a woman suspected of spying for China. The board said senior US officials had told it his return posed no national security risk. Nvidia’s shares rose about 31 per cent and the S&P 500 gained about 4.7 per cent. On Tuesday South Korea’s main index closed 6.3 per cent higher, back above 5,000, and Taiwan’s market jumped nearly 9 per cent in trading.
stories.whatChanged: Huang is back in charge, and the AI share sell-off that had pushed Wall Street into a correction reversed sharply on Monday and across Asia on Tuesday.
stories.whyMatters: Nvidia makes the chips behind most AI systems and carries great weight in stock indexes, so its leadership crisis had become a test of confidence in the whole AI boom, with effects on savings and markets far beyond the United States.
stories.uncertainty: An inquiry into reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort is still under way, and the allegations around his departure are unproven. Reports differ slightly on the size of Monday’s gains, and a single day’s rebound does not show that the sell-off is over.
stories.watchNext: Whether the rebound holds through the Thanksgiving-shortened week on Wall Street, and what the board’s independent investigation finds.
keyFacts: Nvidia’s board voted unanimously on November 23 to reinstate Huang as president, chief executive and director
Nvidia rose 31.4 per cent to about $165 on Monday, adding nearly $1 trillion in market value, City AM reported
The S&P 500 rose about 4.7 per cent on Monday
South Korea’s Kospi closed up 6.32 per cent at 5,006.03 on Tuesday
Colette Kress, who had been interim chief executive, remains finance chief

report.heading: What the board decided
paragraphs: In a statement filed with US regulators, Nvidia said its board had voted unanimously to restore Huang as president, chief executive and director with immediate effect. After a series of conversations with him, the board said, it was satisfied with his candour and his ability to lead. It also said it had taken input from senior levels of the US government and concluded on that basis that his return posed no national security risk.

A committee of independent directors, advised by outside lawyers, will continue investigating reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort; Huang says he supports the inquiry. The board is also setting up a National Security and Export Control Committee of independent directors and is hiring a chief compliance officer. Harvey Jones remains chair.

report.heading: Why he left, and how he came back
paragraphs: Huang stepped down this month after reports of an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset, who was reportedly an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore company suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips into China. He has acknowledged an affair without naming her, and none of the allegations has been proven. As recently as the previous week, Jones told investors there were no plans to bring him back, and City AM reported that the board had at first turned down Huang’s offer to return.

President Trump publicly backed the decision, saying there was no reason to think it posed a risk, and told CNBC he had made a deal to persuade the board. Yahoo Finance reported that the Attorney General had found no evidence of unlawful conduct by Huang.

report.heading: How markets reacted
paragraphs: Chip shares surged with Nvidia on Monday: Micron rose 19 per cent and Intel 16.3 per cent, according to City AM, though Nvidia remained about 5 per cent below its level on the day Huang resigned. On Tuesday the MSCI Asia-Pacific index rose 3.8 per cent, ending an eight-day losing streak that had brought it close to bear-market territory, Asia Times reported. Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and TSMC all climbed sharply, and Japan’s Nikkei was up about 4 per cent in trading.

Governments had already stepped in. South Korea set up a stock stabilisation fund and eased limits on share buybacks for three months, Taiwan banned short selling and used its national stabilisation fund to buy shares, and China’s exchanges lowered the margin requirement for leveraged trades to 80 per cent from 100 per cent.

stories.title: Iran says it will not negotiate until its conditions are met, as Qatar’s prime minister meets Vance and Rubio in Washington
stories.body: Iran’s parliament speaker and chief negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, said on Tuesday that there would be no talks with the United States until seven Iranian conditions were met; Iranian state media say they include ending the naval blockade and lifting sanctions. On Monday Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio met separately with Qatar’s prime minister, who has been carrying messages to Tehran. Iran also said three tankers had struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz despite a US air escort, a claim not independently confirmed.
stories.whatChanged: Tehran has set preconditions for any negotiation, even as Washington’s contacts with the Qatari mediator moved up to the vice president and secretary of state.
stories.whyMatters: With President Trump saying he is inclined to resume major strikes after the new year, the gap between Iran’s terms and American demands will decide whether the blockade ends in a deal or a wider war, and how safe Gulf shipping is in the meantime.
stories.uncertainty: Iran has not published its seven conditions. The mine strikes were described only by Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, and no US response was reported. The expected delay in any US strike rests on unnamed officials quoted by Ynet.
stories.watchNext: Whether Qatar or Pakistan can broker a first step, such as easing disruption in Hormuz in return for limited sanctions relief, before the new year.
keyFacts: Qalibaf said on state television on November 24 that Iran will not negotiate until seven conditions are met
Vance and Rubio met Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani separately on November 23
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards say three tankers struck mines in Hormuz; the claim is unconfirmed
The Joint Maritime Information Centre counts seven tankers hit since November 16, Gulf News reported
Brent crude was below $90 a barrel on November 23, down from more than $103 on November 3

report.heading: Iran’s terms
paragraphs: Qalibaf told state television that Iran would not negotiate with Washington until its seven conditions were met, and warned that Iran could widen the geographical scope of the conflict if its enemies made a mistake, AP reported. The list has not been published; state media say it includes lifting sanctions, ending the blockade and releasing seized assets.

A day earlier, foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei described the sanctions and the blockade as military aggression that gives Iran a right of self-defence under the UN Charter, and said Iran would use every available means against them. He added that security in Hormuz could be restored quickly if the United States kept its commitments.

report.heading: The diplomacy
paragraphs: Vance received Sheikh Mohammed at the White House and Rubio met him at the US–Qatar strategic dialogue. The State Department said only that Rubio thanked Qatar for its mediation. According to AP, mediators are proposing that Iran ease the disruption in Hormuz in exchange for limited sanctions relief, as a step towards broader talks that would include its nuclear programme. Alhurra reported that the two sides disagree on the order of steps, with Washington wanting nuclear limits first, and that Iran’s foreign minister names Qatar and Pakistan as its main indirect channels. AP also reported that Trump told Vance the United States did not need a deal.

report.heading: At sea and in the air
paragraphs: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards navy said three tankers hit mines after breaking its rules for passage through the strait. In a post on Sunday night, Trump said Iran had fired more drones and missiles in the past week than at any time in over a year, and that all had been shot down. Ynet, quoting US officials, reported that any American strike was at least a week away and that Trump leaned towards waiting until after the new year, while Israel’s leaders favour a short, intense joint campaign.

stories.title: NATO gives Poland an early-warning aircraft after the Russian missile incursion, and leaves its other requests to foreign ministers next week
stories.body: Allied ambassadors meeting in Brussels on Monday agreed to put a NATO AWACS surveillance aircraft at Poland’s disposal, Deputy Defence Minister Paweł Zalewski said, after three Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles came down in south-eastern Poland on November 20. Other Polish proposals to strengthen air defence and deterrence, including more allied fighter jets, were put off to a meeting of NATO foreign ministers next week. Zalewski said every ambassador expressed solidarity with Poland. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the incursion a premeditated provocation.
stories.whatChanged: The emergency allied meeting produced one concrete measure, an early-warning aircraft for Poland, and deferred the rest of Warsaw’s requests.
stories.whyMatters: How NATO answers a confirmed Russian cruise missile incursion into an ally shows whether its eastern flank can detect and stop such weapons, and how far allies will go beyond statements of support.
stories.uncertainty: In the reports we read there was no NATO statement or quote from Secretary General Mark Rutte on the meeting’s outcome, and no Russian reaction. Allied early-warning aircraft were already helping to watch Polish airspace, so it is unclear how much the new deployment adds.
stories.watchNext: What NATO foreign ministers decide next week on Poland’s requests for more fighter jets and faster procedures for shooting down incoming missiles.
keyFacts: The North Atlantic Council met in Brussels on Monday, November 23
NATO agreed to put an AWACS early-warning aircraft at Poland’s disposal, Zalewski said
Poland’s other proposals were deferred to a meeting of NATO foreign ministers next week
Poland tracked 11 aerial objects on November 20, three of which crossed the border, Militarnyi reported
Poland has said it will not invoke Article 4 of the NATO treaty

report.heading: What the allies agreed
paragraphs: Zalewski, who represented Poland at Monday’s session of the North Atlantic Council, said allies had granted part of Warsaw’s request by assigning an AWACS aircraft to Poland, and that the remaining proposals for stronger defence and deterrence would go to NATO foreign ministers next week. He said every ambassador had expressed full solidarity, none doubted that Russia had acted deliberately, and all accepted that the alliance’s air defences needed strengthening.

Tusk described the incident as a planned provocation timed to coincide with military exercises nearby. Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said allied early-warning aircraft were already reinforcing surveillance of Polish airspace.

report.heading: What Poland had asked for
paragraphs: Before the meeting, Zalewski told Polsat News that Poland wanted AWACS aircraft and significant air capabilities, but not only those. He also called for a review of NATO procedures so that decisions to shoot down incoming objects can be made faster. Warsaw said it would not invoke Article 4, which provides for formal consultations when an ally feels threatened.

Prosecutors in Lublin have identified all three objects as Kh-101 cruise missiles made this autumn in Dubna, near Moscow. On November 20 Poland tracked 11 aerial objects during a large Russian attack on Ukraine, scrambled Polish F-16s and Swedish Gripens flying for NATO, and activated its Patriot and other air-defence systems.

report.heading: The limits of the response
paragraphs: Defence Matters noted that an AWACS aircraft improves detection but does not replace missile defences or fighters, and that the decision says nothing about whether NATO will change its rules for engaging incoming weapons. Polish authorities have not established that the missiles were aimed at Polish targets. Russia had not commented on the findings in the reports we read.

stories.title: More drones hit Sudan’s capital, and the United States and the UN call for a truce and an end to the flow of weapons
stories.body: A drone strike on homes in Karari, in Khartoum state, killed three people and injured ten, five of them children, on Monday, local authorities said, a day after drones hit homes and a UN building in the capital. Massad Boulos, a senior US adviser, said the attacks had reportedly been launched by the Rapid Support Forces, and called for a quick humanitarian truce and an end to weapons reaching Sudan. The UN’s top official in the country made a similar appeal, and Saudi Arabia and Egypt condemned the strikes.
stories.whatChanged: The drone attacks on Khartoum continued into a second day, and Washington publicly linked them to the Rapid Support Forces and demanded that outside weapons supplies stop.
stories.whyMatters: Strikes on a capital the army recaptured last year, including on a UN building, show the war reaching civilians far from the front lines, and make drones supplied from abroad a central issue for any diplomacy.
stories.uncertainty: Casualty figures for Sunday’s strikes differ: one report counts at least four dead, while AFP said authorities had given no toll. The army’s claim that the drones were launched from Ethiopia is unverified, and Ethiopia has denied similar accusations before.
stories.watchNext: Whether the army or the Rapid Support Forces respond to the call for a truce, and the army’s advance towards En Nahud in West Kordofan.
keyFacts: A drone strike in Karari, Khartoum state, killed 3 people and injured 10 on November 23, local authorities said
Sunday’s strikes killed at least four people in Khartoum, including a 10-year-old, Sudan Tribune reported

Darfur24 reported a drone strike near Armal in West Kordofan that killed at least eight civilians

report.heading: The latest strikes
paragraphs: Monday’s attack in Karari hit civilian areas, local authorities told Anadolu. Khartoum’s governor, Ahmed Othman Hamza, blamed the Rapid Support Forces, which the army calls the militia. On Sunday drones struck homes and a UN building while UN staff were inside; Addis Standard described it as the first reported attack on a UN compound in the capital since the army recaptured it. An unnamed army source said the drones had been launched from an airport in Ethiopia, which has not been independently confirmed.

report.heading: The diplomatic response
paragraphs: Boulos wrote on X that drones supplied from outside Sudan were killing civilians almost every day, and urged a rapid humanitarian truce. Denise Brown, the UN resident coordinator, also called for the flow of weapons into Sudan, and drones in particular, to stop. Saudi Arabia and Egypt condemned the attacks, AFP reported. Neither the army nor the Rapid Support Forces had publicly accepted a truce in the reports we read.

report.heading: The fighting elsewhere
paragraphs: In West Kordofan, where the army is pushing towards the town of En Nahud, Darfur24 reported that a drone hit a passenger vehicle near Armal and killed at least eight civilians; local sources believed it was an army drone, and the date of the strike was not given.

stories.title: Venezuela’s government and opposition end a fourth round of talks without an election date or a new electoral council
stories.body: A US-backed round of talks in Caracas between the government of acting President Delcy Rodríguez and the opposition ended on Monday after about ten days, without agreement on renewing the national electoral council, releasing political prisoners or setting an election date. The two sides did agree to review bans on political parties, to update broadcast licences for six television channels, and to work with British officials to recover Venezuelan gold held at the Bank of England. The next round is due in December.
stories.whatChanged: Opposition hopes of an announcement on a new electoral council were not met, and the round produced only narrower agreements.
stories.whyMatters: A credible timetable for elections is the central test of Venezuela’s transition, and slow progress leaves political prisoners in detention and the rules for future votes undecided.
stories.uncertainty: Reports differ on the next round: one gives December 11, another says only December. It is not clear how soon the agreed reviews will change any laws.
stories.watchNext: The fifth round of talks in December, and whether it begins the renewal of the electoral council.
keyFacts: The fourth round ran from November 13 to November 23 in Caracas
National Assembly president Jorge Rodríguez led the government side and Dinorah Figuera the opposition
Six channels, including Globovisión, Venevisión and the state broadcaster VTV, are to have their licences updated
La Ceiba reported that a fifth round is set for December 11

report.heading: What the round produced
paragraphs: According to EFE, the sides agreed a plan that includes meetings with senior British officials to free Venezuelan gold held at the Bank of England, which has still not been returned. They also agreed to review the cases of barred political parties and to consult on reforming the laws on parties and public demonstrations, to revise the law against hatred and to review the law on organised crime and terrorist financing, which has often been used against protesters. Broadcast concessions for ANTV, Fe y Alegría, Globovisión, VTV, Venevisión and Televen are to be updated.

report.heading: What it did not deliver
paragraphs: The announcements many had expected did not come: no start to replacing the national electoral council, no release of political prisoners and no election date. Figuera had predicted good news on the council before the round closed. La Ceiba reported that she thanked the United States and Secretary of State Marco Rubio for their support, and that relatives of political prisoners have challenged ten nominees for the Supreme Court.

report.heading: Who is at the table
paragraphs: The government side is led by Jorge Rodríguez, president of the National Assembly, on behalf of acting President Delcy Rodríguez. The opposition delegation is led by Figuera, who comes from the National Assembly elected in 2015. The opposition leader María Corina Machado is not part of the talks, EFE reported.

stories.title: The death toll in the Indonesian sweet factory fire rises to 26, with eight workers still missing
stories.whatChanged: Officials now count 26 dead and eight missing after the fire in Banten province, and police are examining the factory’s safety record.
stories.body: The fire broke out on Saturday at a three-storey confectionery plant in Cikande, west of Jakarta, and took about 14 hours to control. Police say the bodies must be identified by DNA, and have questioned 19 witnesses and seized safety documents; many victims were found near an emergency staircase on the second floor. Workers told AP that no alarm sounded, while the company’s chief executive said the plant held regular drills.

stories.title: A Mexican judge orders cartel leader ‘El Chapo Isidro’ held in the Altiplano maximum-security prison
stories.whatChanged: A federal judge ruled Fausto Isidro Meza Flores’s arrest lawful on Monday and ordered him held before trial, with a decision on charges due on Saturday.
stories.body: Meza Flores, who is on the FBI’s most wanted list, appeared by video at a closed hearing of about five hours and is accused of drug and weapons offences. Two alleged associates, a cousin and a brother-in-law, were also sent to the Altiplano prison. The judge will rule on November 28 on whether the three go to trial. Reported deaths from last Friday’s raid in Sinaloa have risen, with Proceso citing four soldiers and 16 attackers killed.

stories.title: Congo, the world’s main source of cobalt, will suspend all cobalt exports from November 30 to lift prices
stories.whatChanged: Congo’s strategic minerals regulator announced an indefinite halt on cobalt exports from industrial and small-scale mines, starting at the end of the month.
stories.body: The regulator, ARECOMS, cited a sharp and lasting fall in prices; cobalt hydroxide has lost nearly half its value since an April peak, according to Fastmarkets data cited by Reuters. It will review the halt after four months and use the pause to rework export quotas. It is Congo’s second blanket suspension, after one that ran from February to October 2025. Cobalt is used in batteries for electric cars and phones.

stories.title: Brazil’s former president Jair Bolsonaro develops pneumonia in intensive care, and doctors rule out surgery for now
stories.whatChanged: Bolsonaro has pneumonia in both lungs on top of a bowel obstruction, his doctors said on Monday.
stories.body: Bolsonaro, 71, developed chills, vomiting and low oxygen levels on Sunday and is on antibiotics in intensive care at a hospital in Brasília, with no discharge date. His doctors said the bowel obstruction had improved and they had chosen treatment without surgery. He is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup, under house arrest; the Supreme Court votes from December 4 on a law that could shorten sentences in the case.

stories.title: Lean’s maintainers certify the AI-assisted Riemann proof as formally correct, as mathematicians begin the slower work of understanding it
stories.body: The organisations behind the Lean proof assistant and its mathematics library say they have certified both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis in Levent Alpöge’s Claude-assisted code. Tools confirmed that the theorem matches the library’s vetted definition exactly, and several independent checkers accepted the proof. A machine check is not the same as human understanding: Terence Tao expects the argument, which appears to draw on the Langlands programme, to take time to digest, and conventional peer review has not begun.
stories.whatChanged: The checks that were still running when we last reported have now passed, according to a statement from Lean’s maintainers dated November 21 that we have now read.
stories.whyMatters: If it holds, a central open problem in mathematics has been settled with the help of an AI system, and in a form a computer can verify even before people can follow it.
stories.hook: The machine verdict is in and it is positive; the human verdict, which decides how mathematics absorbs the result, will take much longer.
stories.uncertainty: Formal certification checks that the stated theorem was proved, not what the proof teaches; no human-readable account of the argument yet exists. One end-to-end comparison was still running on November 23, according to a secondary tracker.
stories.watchNext: Alpöge’s planned written exposition of the proof, and whether number theorists publish their own analyses of its key steps.
keyFacts: The Lean FRO and Mathlib Initiative certified the statement and proof in a joint statement on November 21
Two comparison tools confirmed the theorem matches Mathlib’s vetted definition of the Riemann Hypothesis
An axiom audit found only Lean’s three standard axioms, according to Kingy AI’s account
Under the Clay Institute’s rules, a prize requires publication and two years of community acceptance

report.heading: What was certified
paragraphs: The proof, released by Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge on November 20, runs to about 17 million lines of Lean code. The Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative isolated the theorem statement in a file that relies only on Mathlib, the community’s shared library, and two separate tools confirmed it matches the library’s carefully reviewed definition of the Riemann Hypothesis. That rules out the main worry raised last week: that the code proved something subtly different from the real conjecture.

The proof itself was exported and checked by Lean’s own kernel and by several independent checkers, some written in other programming languages, on a copy isolated from the original source code so that hidden tricks could not interfere.

report.heading: The independent checks
paragraphs: According to Kingy AI’s running account, Andrew Sutherland of MIT compiled more than 175,000 modules and found only Lean’s three standard axioms, a build on the LUMI supercomputer reproduced the same results, and a sandboxed rebuild reproduced the full 61.6-gigabyte export. The same account said one complete end-to-end comparison on the original export was still in progress on November 23.

report.heading: What comes next
paragraphs: Mathematicians now face the task of understanding why the proof works. Terence Tao’s early reading suggests it draws on the Langlands programme and arithmetic geometry, and Michael Rubinstein of the University of Waterloo is preparing a long working draft that breaks a key step into smaller claims. Alpöge plans a written exposition.

stories.title: The FDA approves the first treatment for any form of limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, a daily oral drug
stories.body: The US Food and Drug Administration approved Welgemda, an oral ribitol drug from BridgeBio, for a type of limb-girdle muscular dystrophy caused by faults in the FKRP gene. It is the first approved therapy for any limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, a group of inherited muscle diseases. The approval rests on a planned 12-month interim look at a 112-patient trial that showed better walking speed and lung function than placebo; the trial’s main results are not due until 2027.
stories.whatChanged: Patients with this form of the disease have an approved treatment for the first time.
stories.whyMatters: Limb-girdle muscular dystrophies have had no approved treatment, so this offers patients with one subtype an option, and shows regulators will act on interim data for rare diseases.
stories.hook: A first for a neglected group of muscle diseases, though the approval rests on interim results and covers only one genetic subtype.
stories.uncertainty: The approval is based on interim data; the trial’s main endpoint is at 36 months. The FDA did not publish effect sizes in the reports we read, the price was not disclosed, and the drug’s mechanism is not fully understood.
stories.watchNext: The full results of the FORTIFY trial, expected around 2027, and the drug’s price.
keyFacts: The FDA approved Welgemda for limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2I/R9 on November 23
It is approved for adults and for children weighing at least 30 kilograms
The Phase 3 FORTIFY trial enrolled 112 patients, two for every one on placebo
Walking speed improved by 0.27 metres per second against placebo at 12 months, Reuters reported

report.heading: What was approved
paragraphs: Welgemda, also known as BBP-418, is a ribitol solution taken twice a day by mouth. It is made by ML Bio Solutions and sold by BridgeBio. The FDA approved it for limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2I/R9, which is caused by mutations in the FKRP gene, in adults and in children weighing at least 30 kilograms. AJMC describes it as the first approved therapy for any limb-girdle muscular dystrophy.

report.heading: The evidence
paragraphs: The decision rests on a planned 12-month interim analysis of the Phase 3 FORTIFY trial, which randomised 112 patients two to one against placebo and runs for up to 36 months. Reuters reported that a marker showing the drug reaches its target rose 1.8 times compared with placebo at three months. At 12 months, levels of creatine kinase, a sign of muscle damage, differed significantly, walking speed improved by 0.27 metres per second and lung function was about 5 per cent better than on placebo.
The most common side effects were digestive problems such as diarrhoea and stomach pain, and joint pain.

report.heading: The limits
paragraphs: The trial’s primary endpoint is measured at 36 months, so the full picture will come later. The approval applies only to one genetic subtype, and the drug’s exact mechanism is not fully known.

stories.title: OpenAI’s chief scientist proposes an industry-wide ceiling on AI capability, measured by how well models predict text
stories.body: Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI’s chief scientist, has proposed that leading AI developers agree on a shared yardstick of general capability, based on how accurately models predict the next word in text, and on a ceiling they would not cross until agreed safety milestones are met. In an essay he warns that AI could start to speed up breakthroughs in how models are trained as early as 2027, outpacing safety techniques. Sam Altman praised the essay, but it is not formal company policy and no other lab has signed up.
stories.whatChanged: A senior figure at a leading lab has put forward a concrete mechanism for pacing AI development across companies.
stories.whyMatters: Labs have talked about slowing down if risks grow, but have lacked a shared measure to decide when; a common metric would make any such pact checkable.
stories.hook: An idea, not a commitment: the proposal has no other signatories and leaves open who would measure and enforce it.
stories.uncertainty: We could not open the essay itself and rely on two reports of it. It is unclear who would measure compliance or whether the metric can be compared fairly across different models and data.
stories.watchNext: Whether other leading labs or governments respond to the proposal, or adopt a similar measure.
keyFacts: Pachocki’s essay is titled Perplexity and Intelligence
It proposes perplexity, a measure of next-word prediction, as a common yardstick of capability
It warns that AI could accelerate fundamental training breakthroughs as early as 2027
Sam Altman called it the most important thing OpenAI had published in a while

report.heading: The proposal
paragraphs: In the essay, Pachocki argues that how well a model predicts text, measured as perplexity or loss, tracks its general capability closely enough to serve as a common measure across companies. Leading developers would agree on an initial capability ceiling and stay below it until defined safety milestones were met; one example he gives is a more effective successor to monitoring a model’s chain of reasoning, according to ODSC and The Media Copilot.

report.heading: Why now
paragraphs: Pachocki warns that AI systems could begin to accelerate fundamental advances in pre-training from as early as 2027, which could outrun the techniques used to monitor and control them. The essay’s examples come only from OpenAI’s own models.

The Media Copilot reports that the essay uses those models to illustrate the trend: GPT-4 reached a loss of about 0.91 on the measure, and OpenAI’s systems have since gone below 0.8. In the reports we read, the essay does not set a specific number for the first ceiling.

report.heading: The open questions
paragraphs: The proposal is voluntary and has not been adopted as OpenAI policy, though chief executive Sam Altman praised it. No other developer has agreed to it. It does not set out who would measure compliance or how agreements would be verified.

image.alt: A rising gauge needle stopping just below a copper bar across the top of the dial: a proposed ceiling on how capable AI systems may become.

sources.title: OpenAI Chief Scientist Proposes Industry-Wide AI Limits Based on Perplexity
OpenAI chief scientist proposes perplexity as a way to limit AI development

stories.title: Congo’s Ebola outbreak passes 11,700 confirmed cases, as the WHO says fighting in Ituri is disrupting the response
stories.body: Congo’s Ebola outbreak had reached 11,762 confirmed cases and 5,775 deaths across 68 health zones in eight provinces by November 20, according to figures reported by UN News. Ituri province alone accounts for more than 8,000 cases. The head of the World Health Organization said heavy fighting there had forced health workers to shelter in a hospital maternity ward for more than a day, and that the agency was working on a safe way out. There is no approved vaccine for the Bundibugyo strain behind the outbreak.
stories.whatChanged: Updated figures show the outbreak still growing, and no evacuation of the trapped health workers had been reported.
stories.whyMatters: Ebola is stopped by tracing contacts, isolating patients and treating them, all of which depend on health workers being able to move safely; fighting in the worst-hit province makes each of those harder.
stories.uncertainty: The reports we read did not name the armed group involved or confirm that the team had got out. Official figures lag behind events by several days.
stories.watchNext: Whether the WHO team in Ituri is evacuated safely, and the next update on case numbers.
keyFacts: 11,762 confirmed cases and 5,775 deaths across 68 health zones as of November 20
Ituri has more than 8,000 cases and 3,791 deaths
The WHO has verified more than 87 attacks on health care in Congo this year
There is no approved vaccine for the Bundibugyo strain

report.heading: The state of the outbreak
paragraphs: According to UN News, the outbreak had caused 11,762 confirmed cases and 5,775 deaths in 68 health zones across eight provinces by November 20. Ituri has recorded more than 8,000 cases and 3,791 deaths, a fatality rate of about 47 per cent. The Bundibugyo strain has no approved vaccine, which leaves contact tracing and isolation as the main tools.

report.heading: Fighting around the response
paragraphs: WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on Sunday that responders had taken shelter in a hospital maternity ward in Ituri for more than 24 hours because of heavy fighting, and that the WHO was working to get them out. He said fighting was disrupting the response and called for peace. The WHO has verified more than 87 attacks on health care in Congo this year, and earlier this month the UN’s humanitarian coordinator said fighters of the Allied Democratic Forces had recently killed more people than Ebola.

Without a vaccine, the response relies on finding the contacts of patients and isolating anyone who falls ill, work that depends on teams being able to travel safely. Tedros said the clashes were disrupting that work, Reuters reported, and the WHO said it was trying to arrange a safe exit for the team sheltering in the hospital.

watch.text: NATO foreign ministers meet next week and are due to take up Poland’s remaining requests, including more fighter jets and faster rules for shooting down incoming missiles.

north-america.summary: Nvidia’s reinstatement of Jensen Huang set off one of Wall Street’s biggest one-day rallies, while senators look for ways to limit the Iran war through the December funding deadline.

briefs.title: Senators look to December’s funding deadline to rein in the Iran war
briefs.text: Senator Tim Kaine says he has finished a bill that would bar spending on offensive operations against Iran without approval from Congress, Alhurra reported. Senator Susan Collins is exploring wording that would pay to replenish weapons stocks without funding a continued war. Current government funding runs out on December 11.

sources.title: Rubio Meets Qatari Premier as Iran Diplomacy Continues

latin-america.summary: Venezuela’s talks end another round without an election date, a Mexican judge jails a top cartel suspect, and Jair Bolsonaro’s condition worsens.

briefs.title: Petro calls Colombia’s request to suspend his X account censorship
briefs.text: Former president Gustavo Petro said on Monday that his government’s request to X to suspend his account was an attempt at censorship. The information technology ministry asked for the suspension over possible incitement to violence after Petro urged Colombians to demand President De la Espriella’s immediate resignation. No decision by X had been reported.

africa.summary: Drones strike Sudan’s capital again, Congo halts cobalt exports and its Ebola outbreak grows, and reprisal killings are reported in central Nigeria.

briefs.title: Herders’ group says 64 Fulani were killed in reprisals in Nigeria’s Niger State
briefs.text: After attackers killed a village head and four others in Borgu district on November 21, suspected vigilantes struck two communities in apparent revenge, Daily Trust reported. The state chairman of the herders’ association Miyetti Allah says 64 Fulani were killed and buried, and Wawa residents confirmed a mass burial of 38. Police said they would verify the figures, and the state government had not commented.

briefs.title: Bahrain intercepts more Iranian attacks
briefs.text: Bahrain said its air defences intercepted several Iranian attacks without injuries, after an attack on Saturday hit an industrial site and injured two people, one critically. Iranian media said the Revolutionary Guards were targeting US bases in Bahrain. Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, the UAE, Jordan and the Arab League condemned the attacks.

asia.summary: Asian markets rebound strongly after Nvidia’s reversal, Indonesia’s factory fire toll rises, and Baloch militants claim new attacks in Pakistan.

briefs.title: Baloch militants claim deadly attacks on Pakistani forces
briefs.text: The Balochistan Liberation Army said in a statement on Tuesday that it had killed 20 Pakistani security personnel and alleged informants in attacks on November 21 and 22, including drone strikes on a camp in Nushki. A second group claimed 36 deaths in operations earlier this month. Pakistani officials had not confirmed or denied the claims in the report we read.

oceania.summary: Pacific island governments voice dismay at the failed COP31 talks, while Australia’s opposition keeps up pressure on the climate minister.

briefs.title: Pacific nations say they were let down by the failed climate summit
briefs.text: The Marshall Islands said it had been let down on all sides after COP31 in Antalya ended without an agreement, and Tuvalu’s climate minister, Maina Talia, criticised a lack of transparency. Australia, which co-led the talks, faces opposition claims that its A$150 million outlay was wasted; Prime Minister Anthony Albanese did not say whether Chris Bowen would stay on as climate minister.
